page: Hetzner Cloud ccx63 is a dedicated CPU virtual server powered by the x86_64 AMD EPYC processor architecture. It features 48 dedicated vCPUs derived from 24 physical cores with 2 threads per core, operating at a base clock speed of 2.0 GHz. The processor configuration includes a cache hierarchy of 32 KB L1d, 0.5 MB L2, and 32 MB L3 cache. The system is provisioned with 188.0 GB of system memory, yielding approximately 3.91 GB of RAM per core. Storage is provided via a local 960 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance operates under a QEMU hypervisor. No complimentary public IPv4 addresses are included.

In benchmark evaluations, the ccx63 demonstrates strong multi-core processing capabilities, as evidenced by its stress-ng multi-core CPU score of 73209.23 and a PassMark CPU score of 64305.59, both placing in the top 25%. The server excels in parallelized workloads, achieving strong results in multi-threaded bzip3 decompression (305.9 GB/sec) and software compilation using Clang (46060.0). Cryptographic and mathematical execution is supported by hardware-accelerated AVX, AES, and SHA_NI instruction sets, reflected in a strong PassMark encryption score of 58566.64. Memory performance, however, is moderate, with uncached read and write bandwidths of 148.56 GB/sec and 80.13 GB/sec respectively, aligning with the middle 50% of tested systems.

The combination of 48 dedicated AMD EPYC cores and a local 960 GB NVMe SSD makes this instance highly suitable for database operations and high-throughput key-value stores. This is supported by a strong PassMark database operations score of 22243.57 and Redis SET performance reaching 62.09 million operations per second. While the server lacks a dedicated GPU, it exhibits strong CPU-based LLM inference capabilities, particularly in text generation for small models (360.33 tokens/sec) and medium models (28.13 tokens/sec). Given its dedicated resource allocation and balanced memory-to-core ratio, the ccx63 offers high resource density and cost efficiency for compute-heavy, multi-threaded applications, database hosting, and software build pipelines, though workloads requiring massive memory bandwidth or GPU acceleration may face performance limitations.
